implementation_notes: Swift's own guard statement is the language-level replacement for the guard object: guard policy.decide(context, action, resource) is .allow else { throw AccessDenied(...) } executes the denial path unless the decision allows the operation, and the compiler forces the early exit (The Swift Programming Language, Control Flow: structure code with branches, loops and early exits). The policy is a protocol-typed value with a pure decide method injected into the guarded type. What replaces the classic structure: the guard statement plus protocols replace the Guard class and the virtual policy hierarchy; a generic wrapper type is still justified when one guard must cover many methods uniformly, since repeating the statement at every entry point invites omissions.
idiom_name: guard statement + Policy protocol (denial by thrown error)
pitfalls: guard ... else { fatalError() } crashes the process instead of denying safely; the else branch must throw a mapped error or return a typed failure.
An existential policy (any Policy) boxes and may allocate; if it crosses concurrency domains it must be Sendable, and mutable rule state belongs in an actor.
The guard statement only enforces the methods that contain it; centralise the check in a wrapper type when the resource has many entry points.
